claim: PSD-95 is a scaffold protein that links postsynaptic receptors to sites of presynaptic neurotransmitter release.
source: The scaffold protein PSD-95 links postsynaptic receptors to sites of presynaptic neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing the function of PSD-95.

claim: Flexible linkers between folded domains in PSD-95 enable a dynamic supertertiary structure.
source: Flexible linkers between folded domains in PSD-95 enable a dynamic supertertiary structure.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a property of PSD-95.

claim: Interdomain interactions within the PSG supramodule regulate PSD-95 activity.
source: Interdomain interactions within the PSG supramodule, formed by PDZ3, SH3, and Guanylate Kinase domains, regulate PSD-95 activity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a functional property of the PSG supramodule.

claim: The study combined discrete molecular dynamics and single molecule FRET to characterize the PSG supramodule.
source: Here we combined discrete molecular dynamics and single molecule Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) to characterize the PSG supramodule, with time resolution spanning picoseconds to seconds.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: A FRET network was used to measure distances in full-length PSD-95 and model the conformational ensemble.
source: We used a FRET network to measure distances in full-length PSD-95 and model the conformational ensemble.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: PDZ3 samples two conformational basins.
source: We found that PDZ3 samples two conformational basins, which we confirmed with disulfide mapping.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: The two conformational basins of PDZ3 were confirmed with disulfide mapping.
source: We found that PDZ3 samples two conformational basins, which we confirmed with disulfide mapping.
evidence: This describes the validation method for the conformational basins.

claim: PSD-95 bound neuroligin well at physiological pH.
source: We found that PSD-95 bound neuroligin well at physiological pH while truncated PDZ3 bound poorly.
evidence: This is a primary finding from binding experiments stated in the abstract.

claim: Truncated PDZ3 bound neuroligin poorly at physiological pH.
source: We found that PSD-95 bound neuroligin well at physiological pH while truncated PDZ3 bound poorly.
evidence: This is a primary finding from binding experiments stated in the abstract.

claim: The supertertiary context of PDZ3 enables recognition of neuroligin.
source: Our hybrid structural models reveal how the supertertiary context of PDZ3 enables recognition of this critical synaptic ligand.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural models and binding data.

claim: Most proteins are composed of more than one domain.
source: Most proteins are composed of more than one domain (Ekman et al., 2005; Apic et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: MAGuKs are scaffold proteins that link cell surface membrane proteins to their intracellular signaling partners and the cytoskeleton.
source: MAGuKs are scaffold proteins that link cell surface membrane proteins to their intracellular signaling partners and the cytoskeleton (Ye et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Almost all MAGuKs contain a conserved 'PSG' supramodule.
source: Almost all MAGuKs contain a conserved 'PSG' supramodule that links a Postynaptic Density Protein of 95 kDa, Discs Large, Zonula Occludens-1 (PDZ) domain (Ye and Zhang, 2013) an Src Homology 3 (SH3) domain (Saksela and Permi, 2012) and Guanylate kinase-like (GuK) domain (Kistner et al., 1995; Olsen and Bredt, 2003) that serves as another protein-binding domain (Kim et al., 1997; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The HOOK region within the SH3 domain disrupts canonical SH3 domain interactions.
source: One distinctive feature of the MAGuKs is the insertion of a variable HOOK (Hough et al., 1997) region within the SH3 domain that disrupts canonical SH3 domain interactions (McGee et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PSD-95 contains an N-terminal extension and two tandem PDZ domains attached to its PSG.
source: The postsynaptic density protein of 95 kilodaltons (PSD-95) contains an N-terminal extension and two tandem PDZ domains attached to its PSG (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Twelve cysteine mutations spanning PDZ3, SH3, and GuK were used to probe the location of PDZ3 within the PSG supramodule.
source: To experimentally probe the location of PDZ3 within the PSG supramodule, we used 12 cysteine mutations spanning PDZ3, SH3, and GuK (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The labeling sites were identified in previous work and screened for dye properties.
source: These labeling sites were identified in our previous work, which included screening of dye properties at these sites through measurements of ensemble anisotropy and quantum yield (McCann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: All variants used in this work were homogeneous with respect to their chromatographic properties and monodisperse.
source: All of the variants used in this work were homogeneous with respect to their chromatographic properties and monodisperse as assessed by our size exclusion chromatography before measurements.
evidence: This describes quality control measures for the protein samples.

claim: Twelve variants form a FRET network necessary for structural modeling.
source: By using these labeling sites in different combinations, we created 12 variants (Figure 1C). These variants form a FRET network, which is necessary for structural modeling (Figure 1D; Medina et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the experimental design with reference to figures and a citation.

claim: Two experimental approaches were used to measure smFRET: confocal microscopy with MFD and smTIRF.
source: We used two experimental approaches to measure smFRET. The same batches of purified PSD-95 variants were split for measurements in solution using confocal microscopy with multiparameter fluorescence detection (MFD) and also encapsulated within lipid vesicles for measurements using smTIRF.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: Pulsed-interleaved excitation (PIE) allowed selection of molecules with active donor and acceptor fluorophores.
source: Fluorescently labeled proteins measured with confocal microscopy with pulsed-interleaved excitation (PIE) (Kudryavtsev et al., 2012), which allowed selection of molecules with active donor and acceptor fluorophores (Appendix 1—table 1 and Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology with a citation.

claim: A global fit of all variants was performed assuming one conformational landscape for PSD-95.
source: One of the necessary assumptions in this work is that there is one conformational landscape for PSD-95 (i.e. ground truth) and that each variant provides specific information on the same landscape.
evidence: This describes a key assumption in the data analysis.

claim: A two-state model with a small no FRET population is sufficient to fit all the data from all 12 variants.
source: Thus, based on fitting statistics (Table 1), we conclude that a two-state model with a small no FRET population is sufficient to fit all the data from all 12 variants (Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The two-state model suggests that PDZ3 samples two limiting conformations with slight predominance of state B (53.9%) over state A (46.1%).
source: This two state model suggests that PDZ3 samples two limiting conformations with slight predominance of state B (53.9%) over state A (46.1%).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the global fit of the data.

claim: All measured variants exhibited a rightward skew away from the static FRET-line, a hallmark of conformational dynamics.
source: All measured variants exhibited a rightward skew away from the static FRET-line, a hallmark of conformational dynamics (Figure 3B; Barth et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 3B with a citation.

claim: Variants involving PDZ3 exhibited broad or irregular distributions indicating a heterogeneous conformational ensemble.
source: Variants involving PDZ3 exhibited broad or irregular distributions indicating a heterogeneous conformational ensemble.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: Variants between PDZ3 and SH3 exhibited higher FRET efficiency, suggesting close proximity.
source: Variants between PDZ3 and SH3 exhibited higher FRET efficiency, suggesting close proximity.
evidence: This is an observation from the data with an inference about proximity.

claim: Truncating PSD-95 resulted in broader and more multi-peaked distributions for all variants.
source: Measurements using smTIRF with camera detection revealed changes in the time-averaged FRET distributions for all variants (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1). Truncating PSD-95 resulted in broader and more multi-peaked distributions.
evidence: This is an observation from the smTIRF data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Truncation increased anticorrelated FRET transitions in smTIRF time traces suggesting altered dynamics of PDZ3.
source: Truncation also increased anticorrelated FRET transitions in smTIRF time traces suggesting altered dynamics of PDZ3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from the smTIRF data with an inference about dynamics.

claim: Truncating PSD-95 shifted the limiting state distances for state A and slightly reduced state B occupancy.
source: Truncating PSD-95 shifted the limiting state distances for state A and slightly reduced state B occupancy (Appendix 1—table 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the global fit of the truncated PSG data.

claim: Three decay times were assigned to local motions (tR1), domain reorientations (tR2), and domain exchange (tR3).
source: Three decay times were assigned to local motions (tR1) that maintain residue contacts, domain reorientations (tR2) that alter interdomain interaction interfaces, and domain exchange (tR3) such as large-scale translational exchange between basins (Figure 5A).
evidence: This describes the interpretation of the fFCS data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Replica exchange DMD simulations were performed using 18 replicas with a cumulative total simulation time of 11.9 μs.
source: To map the conformational energy landscape of the truncated PSG supramodule, we performed replica exchange DMD simulations using 18 replicas running at neighboring temperatures with a cumulative total simulation time of 11.9 μs.
evidence: This describes the computational methodology.

claim: An extended starting conformation with PDZ3 not in contact with SH3-GuK was chosen to avoid bias.
source: To avoid bias, we chose an extended starting conformation with PDZ3 not in contact with SH3-GuK (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the initial conditions for the simulations.

claim: PDZ3 primarily adopted a docked medium conformation (α) with a mean Rg of 27.6 Å along with a more compact conformation (β) with mean Rg of 23.4 Å.
source: Instead, the PDZ3 primarily adopted a docked medium conformation (α) with a mean Rg of 27.6 Å along with a more compact conformation (β) with mean Rg of 23.4 Å.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the DMD simulations.

claim: PDZ3 also samples a shallower basin closer to GuK (β-basin), which is separated by an energy barrier of ~2.0 kcal/mol.
source: PDZ3 also samples a shallower basin closer to GuK, which is separated by an energy barrier of ~2.0 kcal/mol (Figure 6C, β-basin).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the DMD simulations shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The α-basin reveals a fuzzy and dynamic interaction with PDZ3 able to reorient around the HOOK helix.
source: Examination of structures within the α-basin reveals a broad ensemble of conformations with PDZ3 able to reorient around the HOOK helix and occasionally sample the SH3 RT loop Kurochkina and Guha, 2013 (Figure 6—figure supplement 3). This suggests a fuzzy and dynamic interaction.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DMD structures with a citation.

claim: Basic residues within HOOK interact with negatively charged residues in PDZ3 and are further stabilized by surface-exposed aromatic and hydrophobic residues in the α-basin.
source: Examination of α-basin pairwise contacts reveals that basic residues within HOOK interact with negatively charged residues in PDZ3 and are further stabilized by surface-exposed aromatic and hydrophobic residues (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of DMD structures shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Steric clashes would preclude PDZ3 from ligand binding while in some conformations within the α-basin.
source: Steric clashes would preclude PDZ3 from ligand binding while in some conformations within the α-basin (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is an inference from the structural analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The PDZ3-SH3 linker interacts with the SH3 domain, which helps retain PDZ3 in the α-basin and prevents more extended conformations.
source: Interestingly, the PDZ3-SH3 linker interacts with the SH3 domain, which helps retain PDZ3 in the α-basin and prevents more extended conformations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DMD simulations.

claim: The β-basin ensemble revealed a more well-defined interaction with PDZ3 binding near the interface of the NMP binding and CORE subdomains of GuK.
source: Examination of the β-basin ensemble revealed a more well-defined interaction with PDZ3 binding near the interface of the nucleoside monophosphate (NMP) binding and CORE subdomains of GuK (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a result from the DMD simulations shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The β-basin interaction does not occlude the canonical peptide binding sites in GuK or PDZ3.
source: The interaction does not occlude the canonical peptide binding sites in GuK or PDZ3 (Figure 6—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is an observation from the structural analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4B.

claim: The β-basin is stabilized by hydrophobic and hydrogen bonding interactions between uncharged polar residues.
source: Analysis of the β-basin pairwise contacts revealed a well-defined binding site stabilized by hydrophobic and hydrogen bonding interactions between uncharged polar residues (Figure 6F) unlike the highly charged interface in the α-basin.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of DMD structures shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Cysteine residues were engineered based on the contact frequency maps to confirm the PDZ3 interactions with SH3 and GuK.
source: To confirm the PDZ3 interactions with SH3 and GuK, we engineered cysteine residues based on the contact frequency maps and measured the extent and rate of disulfide (DS) bond formation (Figure 7).
evidence: This describes the experimental validation approach.

claim: The residue pair N326C-A504C was used to probe the α-basin and are 5.6 Å apart in the α-basin representative.
source: The predominant interface in the α-basin was PDZ3 binding to the HOOK. We probed this basin with the residue pair N326C-A504C, which are only 5.6 Å apart in the α-basin representative (Figure 7A).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for disulfide mapping shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The residue pair G344C-N633C was used to probe the β-basin and are 5.7 Å apart in the β-basin representative.
source: The predominant interface in the β-basin had PDZ3 binding to GuK. We probed this basin with the residue pair G344C-N633C, which are 5.7 Å apart in the β-basin representative (Figure 7B).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for disulfide mapping shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Increased electrophoretic mobility indicated that DS formation was occurring for all samples.
source: Increased electrophoretic mobility indicated that DS formation was occurring for all samples (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the disulfide mapping experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The α-basin variant showed slightly more DS formation than the β-basin variant in full-length PSD-95 but the rates of DS formation were similar.
source: The α-basin variant showed slightly more DS formation than the β-basin variant in full-length PSD-95 but the rates of DS formation were similar (Figure 7E & F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the disulfide mapping experiments shown in Figure 7E and F.

claim: The truncation increased the rate of DS formation for the α-basin variant by ~30%.
source: Interestingly, the truncation had opposite effects on the kinetics of DS formation for the two variants. The rate of DS formation for the α-basin variant increased by ~30% while rate of DS formation for the β-basin variant decreased by sixfold.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the disulfide mapping experiments.

claim: The truncation decreased the rate of DS formation for the β-basin variant by sixfold.
source: Interestingly, the truncation had opposite effects on the kinetics of DS formation for the two variants. The rate of DS formation for the α-basin variant increased by ~30% while rate of DS formation for the β-basin variant decreased by sixfold.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the disulfide mapping experiments.

claim: Variant P3-S2 formed DS albeit much more slowly than either designed variant.
source: DMD simulations found that variant P3-S2 occasionally sampled close distances in the α-basin. As predicted, variant P3-S2 formed DS albeit much more slowly than either designed variant.
evidence: This is a result from the disulfide mapping experiments that validates the DMD predictions.

claim: Variant P1-G2 failed to show any evidence of DS formation even after 1 hr.
source: In contrast, our mid FRET variant, which is not involved in contacts in either basin, failed to show any evidence of DS formation even after 1 hr.
evidence: This is a negative result from the disulfide mapping experiments.

claim: DS analysis confirms that the contact interfaces from DMD are sampled in full-length and truncated PSD-95.
source: Thus, DS analysis confirms that the contact interfaces from DMD are sampled in full-length and truncated PSD-95.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the disulfide mapping experiments.

claim: FRET distances from the global lifetime fits were used as restraints in rigid body docking.
source: To describe the conformation of each limiting FRET state, we used the FRET distances from the global lifetime fits as restraints in rigid body docking.
evidence: This describes the structural modeling approach.

claim: For state A, the best-fit models showed some divergence with PDZ3 near the HOOK insertion but also extended away from the HOOK in conformations lacking interdomain contacts.
source: For state A, the best-fit models showed some divergence with PDZ3 near the HOOK insertion but also extended away from the HOOK in conformations lacking interdomain contacts (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a result from the rigid body docking shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The best-fit models for state B are more tightly clustered and position PDZ3 near the NMP subdomain of GuK.
source: The best-fit models for state B are more tightly clustered and position PDZ3 near the NMP subdomain of GuK (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a result from the rigid body docking shown in Figure 8B.

claim: When more than seven variants were used in the FRET network robustness analysis, the robustness deviation was less than 10% regardless of which variants were included in the subset.
source: When more than seven variants were used, the robustness deviation was less than 10% regardless of which variants were included in the subset.
evidence: This is a result from the FRET network robustness analysis.

claim: The boundaries of α-basin ensemble are enumerated by the variance of the FNR distributions and arise from the conformational fuzziness of interdomain interactions between PDZ3 and SH3.
source: The boundaries of α-basin ensemble are enumerated by the variance of the FNR distributions (Figure 8C) but arise from the conformational fuzziness of interdomain interactions between PDZ3 and SH3 (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FRET network robustness analysis shown in Figure 8C and 8E.

claim: The β-basin is not fuzzy.
source: In contrast, the β-basin is not fuzzy (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the structural analysis shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Principal component analysis was performed and the basins were projected along the first two principal components using the simulated interdomain distances and the FRET distances between PDZ3 and SH3-GuK.
source: We performed principal component analysis and projected the basins along the first two principal components (PC1 and PC2) using the simulated interdomain distances and the FRET distances between PDZ3 and SH3-GuK, which were rescaled such that the integrated volume of each basin was equivalent to its experimental population fraction (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the analysis method shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: PC1 separated the α- and β-basins mostly by interdomain displacement, while PC2 describes the α-basin FRET degeneracy due to domain reorientations within a single basin.
source: PC1 separated the α- and β-basins mostly by interdomain displacement, while PC2 describes the α-basin FRET degeneracy due to domain reorientations within a single basin (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the principal component analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claim: All structural ensembles and kinetic exchange parameters were deposited at PDB-Dev with the IDs: PDBDEV_00000161 and PDBDEV_00000164.
source: Finally, to validate the proposed structural models, we used disulfide mapping and probed interfaces corresponding to the preferred structural basins. In a refinement step, we introduced the disulfide information for both structural modeling approaches.
evidence: This describes the data deposition.

claim: A 10 residue C-terminal neuroligin peptide (NL10) has been reported to bind truncated PDZ3 with an equilibrium dissociation constant (KD) of 10 µM.
source: To compare binding between the truncated PDZ3 and full-length PSD-95, we used a 10 residue C-terminal neuroligin peptide (NL10), which has been reported to bind truncated PDZ3 with an equilibrium dissociation constant (KD) of 10 µM (Saro et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A KD of 25±4 µM was obtained for NL10 binding to truncated PDZ3 at pH 6.
source: We used this peptide N-terminally-labeled with fluorescein and measured fluorescence anisotropy. We obtained a KD of 25±4 µM at pH 6, which is in good agreement given our higher ionic strength.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the binding experiments.

claim: The KD for NL10 binding to truncated PDZ3 increased to over 200 µM at pH 7.4.
source: Surprisingly, we were unable to reach saturation when we repeated this measurement at pH 7.4 indicating that the KD increased to over 200 µM (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the binding experiments shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Neuroligin binding showed a strong pH dependence.
source: Thus, neuroligin binding showed a strong pH dependence.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the binding experiments.

claim: Binding to PDZ3 was poor at physiological pH.
source: Binding to PDZ3 was poor at physiological pH.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the binding experiments.

claim: Full length PSD-95 gave a KD of 15±1 µM at pH 6 and pH 7.4 for NL10 binding.
source: In contrast to truncated PDZ3, full length PSD-95 gave a KD of 15±1 µM at pH 6 and pH 7.4 suggesting the NL10 interaction is enhanced by the supertertiary environment of PDZ3.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the binding experiments.

claim: The NL10 interaction is enhanced by the supertertiary environment of PDZ3.
source: In contrast to truncated PDZ3, full length PSD-95 gave a KD of 15±1 µM at pH 6 and pH 7.4 suggesting the NL10 interaction is enhanced by the supertertiary environment of PDZ3.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the binding experiments.

claim: The PSG showed a KD of 39±1 µM at pH 6 for NL10 binding.
source: Next, we examined neuroligin binding to the PSG truncation. We measured a KD of 39±1 µM at pH 6 suggesting that binding affinity is somewhat reduced in the PSG relative to full length or even the PDZ3 truncation.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the binding experiments.

claim: The PSG showed a KD of 31±2 µM at pH 7.4 for NL10 binding.
source: The PSG showed slightly higher binding affinity at pH 7.4 with a KD of 31±2 µM in stark contrast to the reduced binding affinity of the truncated PDZ3.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the binding experiments.

claim: Effects of truncation on supertertiary structure and dynamics impact NL10 binding.
source: Thus, effects of truncation on supertertiary structure and dynamics impact NL10 binding.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the binding experiments.

claim: Docking of NL10 to truncated PDZ3 at pH 6 identified electrostatic interactions between protonated histidines in NL10 and acidic residues in the PDZ3 β2-β3 loop.
source: To understand this phenomenon, we performed docking of NL10 to truncated PDZ3 at pH 6. We identified electrostatic interactions between protonated histidines in NL10 and acidic residues in the PDZ3 β2-β3 loop (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the docking analysis shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: At pH 7.4, unprotonated histidines are incapable of interacting with negatively charged residues, which explains the pH sensitivity.
source: At pH 7.4, unprotonated histidines are incapable of interacting with negatively charged residues, which explains the pH sensitivity.
evidence: This is an inference from the docking analysis.

claim: Some α-basin conformations block peptide binding due to steric clashes.
source: Some α-basin conformations block peptide binding due to steric clashes.
evidence: This is an observation from the structural analysis.

claim: Docking of NL10 to α-basin structures identified multiple PSG conformations where the acidic residues in PDZ3 interacted with basic residues in HOOK without steric clashes for NL10.
source: However, docking of NL10 to α-basin structures identified multiple PSG conformations where the acidic residues in PDZ3 interacted with basic residues in HOOK without steric clashes for NL10 (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is a result from the docking analysis shown in Figure 10C.

claim: Salt-bridges have a smaller desolvation penalty than unsatisfied charges, which explains why the peptide binds full-length PSD-95 (and PSG) better than truncated PDZ3 at pH7.4.
source: Salt-bridges have a smaller desolvation penalty than unsatisfied charges, which explains why the peptide binds full-length PSD-95 (and PSG) better than truncated PDZ3 at pH7.4.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural and binding data.

claim: The supertertiary context of PDZ3 enables recognition of a critical physiological ligand.
source: Thus, the supertertiary context of PDZ3 enables recognition of a critical physiological ligand.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the binding and structural data.

claim: Proteomic analysis of PSD-95 complexes purified from mouse brain identified 301 different proteins.
source: Proteomic analysis of PSD-95 complexes purified from mouse brain identified 301 different proteins (Fernández, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Kinetic analysis showed that higher-order interactions between proteins bound to PSD-95, play a role in scaffolding activity.
source: Kinetic analysis showed that higher-order interactions between proteins bound to PSD-95, play a role in scaffolding activity (McCann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: DMD and modeling based on FRET distances were in excellent agreement on the location of PDZ3 within two non-overlapping basins.
source: Here we used our combination of experimental and computational methods for dynamic structural biology (Figure 2) to describe the supertertiary structure and dynamics of the conserved PSG supramodule within full-length PSD-95. Multiparameter fluorescence analysis revealed a complex and dynamic conformational landscape. DMD and modeling based on FRET distances were in excellent agreement on the location of PDZ3 within two non-overlapping basins.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the combined experimental and computational analysis.

claim: Both DMD and FRET agree that the α-basin was degenerate due to the fuzzy interface allowing PDZ3 reorientation.
source: Both DMD and FRET agree that the α-basin was degenerate due to the fuzzy interface allowing PDZ3 reorientation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the combined experimental and computational analysis.

claim: Within each basin, each domain undergoes rapid local motion.
source: Within each basin, each domain undergoes rapid local motion.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the correlation analysis.

claim: Reorientation of PDZ3 and sampling of extended states is slower while basin exchange takes place on timescales approaching seconds.
source: Reorientation of PDZ3 and sampling of extended states is slower while basin exchange takes place on timescales approaching seconds, as captured by smTIRF.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the correlation analysis and smTIRF data.

claim: The models were in excellent agreement with SAXS and NMR experiments, which identified multiple conformations with PDZ3 localized predominantly near the HOOK insertion.
source: Our models were in excellent agreement with SAXS and NMR experiments, which identified multiple conformations with PDZ3 localized predominantly near the HOOK insertion and suggested involvement of residues around the PDZ3 peptide binding pocket (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature supported by a citation.

claim: Previous Rosetta modeling suggested the PDZ3-SH3 linker bridged the interaction while DMD simulations suggested the PDZ3-SH3 interaction was direct.
source: However, the previous Rosetta modeling of linker suggested the PDZ3-SH3 linker bridged the interaction while DMD simulations suggested the PDZ3-SH3 interaction was direct.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature.

claim: The PDZ3-SH3 linker is almost 100% conserved in PSD-95 homologues from humans to Drosophila.
source: In DMD simulations, the linker interacts with SH3 and GuK to help retain PDZ3. This linker is almost 100% conserved in PSD-95 homologues from humans to Drosophila, which would be unusual unless involved in protein interactions since disordered linkers usually show reduced sequence conservation (Chen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an observation about sequence conservation with a citation.

claim: Neither basin relied on canonical ligand binding modes for the primary interaction.
source: Neither basin relied on canonical ligand binding modes for the primary interaction as suggested by comparative patch analysis (Korkin et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature supported by a citation.

claim: Neither basin corresponded to the position for PDZ3 that was previously identified as the time-averaged location using smTIRF.
source: Additionally, neither basin corresponded to the position for PDZ3 that we previously identified as the time-averaged location using smTIRF (McCann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work by the authors supported by a citation.

claim: The crystal structure of the PSG supramodule from ZO-1 revealed a lack of interdomain interactions.
source: The crystal structure of the PSG supramodule from ZO-1, a MAGuK protein found at intercellular tight junctions, revealed a lack of interdomain interactions (Nomme et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The PDZ3-SH3 linker in ZO-1 is much shorter than PSD-95, which may prevent access to these binding sites.
source: The PDZ3-SH3 linker in ZO-1 is much shorter than PSD-95, which may prevent access to these binding sites.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison with ZO-1.

claim: The basic residues in HOOK and acidic residues in PDZ3 are conserved among synaptic MAGuK homologs PSD-93, SAP97, and SAP102.
source: In contrast, the basic residues in HOOK and acidic residues in PDZ3 are conserved among synaptic MAGuK homologs PSD-93, SAP97, and SAP102 as are most pairwise contacts in the β-basin (e.g., F339-Q594, L342-Q603).
evidence: This is an observation about sequence conservation.

claim: The supertertiary landscape is conserved in synaptic MAGuK homologs as suggested by previous smTIRF measurements.
source: This explains why the supertertiary landscape is conserved in these homologues as suggested by previous smTIRF measurements (McCann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Measurements of CRIPT binding to PDZ3 suggested that PDZ3 adopted two interconverting conformational states in the PSG with different kinetics but the same equilibrium affinity.
source: These supertertiary interactions also affect other ligands. Measurements of CRIPT binding to PDZ3 suggested that PDZ3 adopted two interconverting conformational states in the PSG with different kinetics but the same equilibrium affinity (Laursen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Full-length PSD-95 from Rattus norvegicus was expressed in the Rosetta 2 strain of E. coli.
source: The full-length PSD-95 from Rattus norvegicus, the PSG truncation (residues 303–274) and truncated PDZ3 (303–415) were expressed in the Rosetta 2 strain of E. coli (EMD Millipore) and purified by a combination of Ni-affinity, ion exchange and size exclusion chromatography as previously described for these exact protein constructs (McCann et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology with a citation.

evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: For MFD, proteins were first labeled with a 1:2 ratio of Alexa 488 C5 maleimide followed by addition of a 5:1 molar ratio of Alexa Fluor 647 C2 maleimide.

evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: Two experimental setups were used for confocal measurements to obtain MFD data.

claim: Both setups utilized pulsed interleaved excitation (PIE) to alternately excite donor and acceptor fluorophores directly.

source: The PDZ3 and SH3-GuK domains of the PSG core were reconstructed using homology modeling of I-TASSER (Iterative Threading ASSEmbly Refinement) hierarchical approach using multiple threading alignments and iterative structural assembly simulations.

claim: The backbone of the GuK domain was kept static while the SH3 and PDZ3 domains were kept flexible in DMD simulations.

claim: Replica exchange DMD simulations were performed with 18 neighboring replicas in the temperature range of 275–360 K.
source: Replica exchange DMD (rxDMD) simulations were performed with 18 neighboring replicas in the temperature range of 275–360 K to efficiently sample the conformational free energy landscape.
evidence: This describes the computational methodology.

claim: Each replica simulation lasted for 660 ns that resulted in a total simulation time of ~11.9 μs.
source: Each replica simulation lasted for 660 ns that resulted in a total simulation time of ~11.9 μs.
evidence: This describes the computational methodology.

source: The last 400 ns trajectories from all 18 replicas were used for the WHAM analysis.
evidence: This describes the computational methodology.

claim: Neuroligin is a known binding partner of PDZ3.
source: Surprisingly, these supertertiary interactions in full-length PSD-95 allowed PDZ3 to interact with the synaptic adhesion protein neuroligin, a known binding partner of PDZ3 (Irie et al., 1997; Fu et al., 2003; Saro et al., 2007), while the truncated domain showed weaker binding.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.
